paragraphs.text: IX.A. Steep Turns
Introduction
How
Maximum Performance Turn
A plane’s maximum turning performance is its fastest rate of turn and shortest radius of turn
This changes with both airspeed and angle of bank
The higher the airspeed, the bigger the radius and the slower the rate
The higher the bank angle, the smaller the radius and the higher the rate
In addition to other factors, the maximum bank angle is determined by the limiting load factor which can be maintained without stalling or exceeding the airplane’s structural limitations
In most small airplanes the max bank is approximately 50o to 60o
The Science Behind It 										AI.IX.A.K3
What makes an airplane turn?
As an aircraft banks lift is divided into a horizontal as well as a vertical component
The horizontal component of lift pulls the aircraft through the turn
The vertical component of lift must be increased to maintain altitude
Bank Angle, Load Factor & Stall Speed 							AI.IX.A.K3d
Basics
Load factor is the result of two forces: Centrifugal force & Weight
Assuming level flight, as bank angle increases, the load factor and stall speed also increase
The opposite also applies – decreasing bank angle decreases load factor and stall speed
Load Factors
As bank increases beyond 45o, the loads on the aircraft increase rapidly
60o bank = load factor of 2 Gs
70o bank = approximately 3 Gs
Stall Speed
Stall speed increases in proportion to the square root of the load factor
Ex. In a 3G turn, a plane that normally stalls at 50 KIAS will stall at about 85 knots
RM: Adverse Yaw (RM: Uncoordinated flight) 						AI.IX.A.R5
When banking, lift and drag are increased on the raised wing, and decreased on the lowered wing
The difference in drag between the wings results in yaw in the opposite the direction of the turn
To counter adverse yaw, rudder is applied with aileron in the direction of the turn
RM: Torque Effect (RM: Uncoordinated flight) 				AI.IX.A.K3a, AI.IX.A.R5
Newton’s 3rd Law – every action has an equal and opposite reaction
The internal engine parts and propeller are revolving in one direction (clockwise / right), an equal force is trying to rotate the airplane in the opposite direction (counterclockwise / left)
Acts around the longitudinal axis, resulting in a roll to the left
Torque Effect in Turns
Torque is based on the speed the engine/propeller are rotating
The higher the power setting, the greater the turning tendency
Trim tabs combat torque effect in cruise on most small planes
Thus, torque effect is generally negligible in a steep turn
Large power changes could require bank adjustments though
Left Turn
Torque, as a left rolling tendency, encourages a left turn
Combined with other left turning tendencies, it can result in a skid
Increase right rudder/reduce left rudder to counter the skid
Right Turn
Torque, as a left rolling tendency, discourages a right turn
Combined with other left turning tendencies, it can result in a slip
Increase right rudder/reduce left rudder to counter the slip
Turn Rate & Radius 										AI.IX.A.K3e
Turn Rate: Degrees per second the aircraft is turning
Affected by both the bank angle and airspeed
As bank angle increases, so does the rate of turn
As airspeed increases, the rate of turn decreases
Turn Radius: Size of circle an aircraft would fly during a turn
Also affected by both the bank angle and airspeed – but opposite to turn rate
As bank angle increases, the radius of turn decreases
As airspeed increases, the radius of turn increases
Overbanking Tendency 									AI.IX.A.K3b
As the turn radius gets smaller, a difference develops between the speed of the inside & outside wing
Outside wing travels a longer path in the same amount of time as the inside wing, and thus generates more lift
Difference in lift can increase bank
Shallow Bank: Lift differential is overcome by lateral stability
Medium Bank: Lift differential matches lateral stability
High Bank: Lift differential outweighs lateral stability
Aircraft continues to bank even with neutral flight controls
Aileron pressure is required in the direction opposite the turn to maintain bank angle
Maneuvering Speed (VA) 									AI.IX.A.K3c
Maximum speed at which the aircraft will stall prior to exceeding airframe limitations
Above VA, full control deflection can lead to stresses greater than the plane is designed to handle
Weight Changes (Bold Method Video)
VA increases with weight - This means the aircraft can maneuver at higher speeds when heavy
The higher the weight, the higher the AOA needed to maintain level flight
Wing is closer to the critical AOA meaning it takes less back pressure (or G load) before a stall
Less ability to put excess Gs on the airframe
Perform all maneuvers, steep turns included, at or below VA
Performing the Steep Turn 								AI.IX.A.K1, AI.IX.A.K2
Before Starting
Select an altitude – No lower than 1,500’ AGL
Pre-maneuver checklist
RM: Clearing turns (especially important due to rapid rate of turn) 			AI.IX.A.R2
Establish the recommended entry airspeed, or a speed that does not exceed VA
Ensure the aircraft is in straight-and-level flight and trimmed
Entering the Turn
Note the entry heading and a visual reference to roll out on
Smoothly roll into the desired bank angle – 45o (Private); 50o (Commercial)
RM: Coordination - Simultaneously apply rudder to maintain coordination 		AI.IX.A.R5
Uncoordinated entries & changing rudder pressure in the turn overcomplicates the maneuver
Passing about 30o of bank, add back pressure to maintain altitude, and power for airspeed
Establish pitch / bank with visual references, crosscheck on the instruments
Establish opposite aileron as necessary
Trim as necessary
During the Turn
RM: Do not focus or stare at any one object (RM: Division of attention) 			AI.IX.A.R1
Awareness of the horizon relative to the nose/wings is necessary to maintain altitude & orientation
90% outside, 10% inside
Loss of orientation
Orientation is not just the bank/pitch attitude but where you are and what is around you
Note the entry heading and select a visual reference point, continue to scan for traffic
Glance at the heading indicator and check visual references to know where you are in the turn
Adjustments
Increasing/Decreasing Altitude
Relax or increase elevator pressure as appropriate
Small changes. Large changes lead to fast movement and a yo-yo effect
Power should be adjusted to maintain airspeed
Changes in bank may also be used to control altitude deviations
Increasing bank decreases lift; Decreasing bank increases lift
1o to 3o of bank stays within bank tolerances
Bank Angle
Adjust bank to maintain the required bank angle, pitch will likely need adjusted as well
If bank is shallow, increase bank and add back pressure to maintain altitude, and vice versa
Roll Out
General rule: Begin the rollout approximately ½ the bank angle from your entry heading (~20o)
Time the rollout so the wings reach level flight on the heading from which the maneuver was started
Gradually reduce back pressure and power as bank is decreased
If elevator was trimmed up, remove the trim during the rollout to prevent a large increase in altitude
Maintain orientation (know where you are in the turn)
Common Errors 										AI.IX.A.K4
Not clearing the area
Inadequate pitch control on entry or rollout
Gaining or losing altitude
Failure to maintain constant bank angle
Poor flight control coordination
Ineffective use of trim
Ineffective use of power
Inadequate airspeed control
Becoming disoriented
Performing by reference to the flight instruments rather than visual references
Failure to scan for other traffic during the maneuver
Attempting to start recovery prematurely
Failure to stop the turn on the designated heading
RM: Hazards (RM: Division of Attention, Distractions, SA & Disorientation, Task Prioritization)
Dividing Attention 										AI.IX.A.R1
90% outside, 10% inside
Crosscheck focus is primarily on outside references with glances inside for airspeed, altitude, etc.
Orientation doesn’t just include aircraft attitude, but also where you are and what/who is around you
Includes airspace, terrain, traffic, etc.
Know what the airplane is doing and where you are (outside references are very helpful)
Distractions 											AI.IX.A.R4
They’re dangerous – remove them from view (if it’s a person, explain the situation and ask them to stop)
High task saturation in steep turns can lead to altitude changes, loss of orientation & inability to clear
Aviate, navigate, communicate
Situational Awareness & Disorientation 							AI.IX.A.R4
High turn rate & G force make disorientation/loss of SA more likely in steep turns than many maneuvers
Note entry heading on the heading indicator as well as by a visual outside reference
Maintain SA & orientation
Know where you are, what’s coming next – Stay ahead of the airplane & be aware of other traffic
If disoriented, stop the maneuver, admit the problem, and take action to regain SA/orientation
Get to a safe attitude, airspeed, and altitude
Task Prioritization 										AI.IX.A.R4
A lot happens quickly during a steep turn, but safely flying the aircraft comes first
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, & communicating
No one responsibility should take full attention for more than a short period
Establish a crosscheck and be very familiar with visual references
Understand what needs to be accomplished when
Recognize when you’re behind and find a way to catch up
Low Altitude Maneuvering 									AI.IX.A.R3
A small problem at high altitude can quickly become a big problem at a low altitude
Be aware of, and avoid, obstructions, towers, etc.
Quick, panicked maneuvers, especially if slow, can result in a stall/loss of control near the ground
Low Altitude Stall/Spin
A low altitude stall or spin can leave little to no recovery time
ALWAYS maintain coordination, and airspeed at low altitudes
If you get any indication of a stall at low level, recover, and climb to a safe altitude
Spin - A result of a stall + yaw
Prevention
Maintain coordination
Do not use abrupt, excessive pressure inputs (especially back elevator pressure)
Stop whatever you’re doing and recover at the first sign of a stall
Recovery (PARE)
Power - Idle
Ailerons - Neutral
Rudder - Full rudder opposite the spin direction
Elevator - Brisk, positive forward pressure (nose down)
When the spin stops, neutralize rudder & raise the nose, being careful not to stall again
Different aircraft respond differently to spins and spin recoveries, follow the POH procedures
CFIT (Controlled Flight into Terrain) - AC 61-134: General Aviation CFIT Awareness
The solution to combating CFIT accidents starts on the ground
Common themes include proper planning, good decision making, and being able to safely operate the aircraft throughout its entire operating range
Recommendations:
Non-instrument rated VFR pilots should not attempt to fly in IMC
Know and fly above minimum published safe altitudes
If IFR, fly published procedures
Verify proper altitude, especially at night or overwater, through use of a correctly set altimeter
Verify all ATC clearances. Question potentially hazardous clearances
Maintain situational awareness both vertically and horizontally
Comply with appropriate regulations for your specific operation
Don't operate below minimum safe altitudes if uncertain of position or ATC clearance
Be extra careful when operating in an area which you are not familiar
Use current charts, appropriate checklists, and know your aircraft and its equipment
Collision Hazards 										AI.IX.A.R2
Collision Avoidance
Scanning
Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Each movement should not exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
Clearing Procedures
Climb/Descent: Use gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Prior to any turn: Clear in the direction of the turn
Maneuvers: Clearing turns – Clear above/below/in front/behind and during maneuvers
Operation Lights On - Voluntary FAA safety program
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night
Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113)
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging Aircraft
Same Category Aircraft: The aircraft to the right has the right-of-way
Different Categories: Basically, the less maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way
Balloons, gliders, and airships have the right of way over airplanes
An aircraft towing or refueling an aircraft has the right-of-way over engine driven aircraft
Approaching Head-on: Each pilot shall alter course to the right
Overtaking: Aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way; when overtaking, pass on the right
Landing
Aircraft landing/on final to land have the right-of-way over those in flight or on the surface
When 2 or more aircraft are approaching for landing, the lower aircraft has the right-of-way
Don’t take advantage of either of these rules
Terrain
Study terminal charts and IFR/VFR chart altitudes, use Max Elevation Figures (MEFs)
Day vs Night flying over terrain
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
Obstacles & Wire Strike
Research obstacles near airports (Terminal Procedures, NOTAMs, etc.)
Antenna Towers can reach > 1,000-2,000’ AGL with supporting guys wires 1,500’ horizontally
Overhead Wires (may not be lit)
Overhead transmission wires and lines span departures and landmarks pilots often follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc.
Conclusion: Brief review of the main point

WHAT
The steep turn maneuver consists of a constant altitude turn in either direction, using a bank angle between 45o to 60o (45o - Private, or 50o - Commercial). This will cause an overbanking tendency during which maximum turning performance is attained and relatively high load factors are imposed.

WHY                                                                             AI.IX.A.K1
Steep turns develop smoothness, coordination, orientation to outsides references, division of attention between control inputs and the constant need to scan for traffic, and control techniques necessary for the execution of maximum performance turns. 
The pilot also understands the effects of the over banking tendency and how to counter it.

Maintain situational awareness both vertically and horizontally
Comply with appropriate regulations for your specific operation

Collision Avoidance
Scanning

Introduction
How
Steep Spirals & Emergency Landings 							AI.IX.B.K2
Trains the pilot to efficiently manage an engine failure and set themself up for a successful, controlled landing
In the case of an engine failure, proceed directly to an emergency landing airport/area
Arriving with too much altitude, the pilot can apply the steep spiral to:
Lose altitude while remaining directly over the landing zone
Control and plan the descent to enter downwind at the most suitable altitude based on conditions
Perform a controlled power-off 180 landing
Rules 											AI.IX.B.K3, AI.IX.B.K4
Maintain an equal radius turn around a point – Approximately ¼ mile is a good reference
The radius should be such that the steepest bank will not exceed 60o
The smaller the radius, the higher the required bank
Turn Radius
Affected by bank angle and airspeed
As airspeed increases, radius increases
As bank angle increases, radius decreases
To maintain a constant radius, bank ties directly to groundspeed
Higher groundspeed = higher bank & vice versa
Enter on the downwind
Highest groundspeed establishes steepest bank at the start
Continue through three 360o spirals
Should not continue below 1,500’ AGL unless performing an emergency landing in conjunction
Triple the approximate altitude lost per turn and add 1,500’ to plan a minimum entry altitude
Clear the engine when headed into the wind (minimizes variation in groundspeed and radius)

Before Starting
Establish the required altitude
Select a ground reference point

Should be in a sparsely populated area that permits an emergency landing

Close the throttle, establish the recommended airspeed, trim the aircraft

Technique: Once the point disappears, wait a few seconds, and start the turn when past the reference point, establishing the ¼ radius (early turn puts you over the point)
Establish the initial bank angle and establish the proper site picture with the reference point
45o bank is a good starting point
Discuss the site picture for your aircraft
During the Spiral
Divide attention between the ground reference point/site picture, other references, & the instruments
Monitor altitude lost during each turn to establish the final 360 and plan a pattern entry
RM: Wind Correction (RM: Effects of wind) 						AI.IX.B.R6
Adjust bank based on changing winds during the descent to maintain a uniform radius
The higher the groundspeed, the steeper the bank required, and vice versa
Higher speeds = bigger radius, therefore bank must be increased with a tailwind
As the airplane transitions into a headwind, bank must be decreased
Wind direction and speed may change during the descent
Adjust to maintain the ¼ mile radius site picture
Airspeed Correction
Inconsistent airspeeds vary the turn radius and therefore the bank required
Adjust pitch to maintain speed – Use small, smooth, proactive changes

Uncoordinated flight results in additional drag and airspeed changes
Failure to hold a constant airspeed varies turn radius and the required bank angle
Do not use rudder to increase/decrease the rate of turn to adjust the ground track

After three complete rotations, roll out within 10o of the entry heading
Maintain orientation - Techniques: Bug the entry heading & count the turns out loud
There should be no change in airspeed transitioning to the straight glide
Be smooth, controlled, and coordinated

Inadequate pitch control on entry or rollout
Not correcting the bank angle to compensate for wind
Poor flight control coordination
Ineffective use of trim
Inadequate airspeed control
Becoming disoriented
Performing by reference to the flight instruments rather than visual references
Not scanning for other traffic during the maneuver
Not completing the turn on the designated heading or reference

Crosscheck focus is primarily on outside references with glances inside for airspeed, altitude, etc.

Introduction
How
Aerodynamics Recap 										AI.IX.C.K2
Maneuvering Speed (VA) 									AI.IX.C.K2c
Maximum speed at which the aircraft will stall prior to exceeding airframe limitations
Above VA, full control deflection can lead to stresses greater than the plane is designed to handle
Weight Changes (Bold Method Video)
VA increases with weight - This means the aircraft can maneuver at higher speeds when heavy
The higher the weight, the higher the AOA needed to maintain level flight
Wing is closer to the critical AOA meaning it takes less back pressure (or G load) before a stall
Less ability to put excess Gs on the airframe
Perform all maneuvers, steep turns included, at or below VA

Basics
Load factor is the result of two forces: Centrifugal force & Weight
Assuming level flight, as bank angle increases, the load factor and stall speed also increase
The opposite also applies – decreasing bank angle decreases load factor and stall speed
Load Factors
As bank increases beyond 45o, the loads on the aircraft increase rapidly
60o bank = load factor of 2 Gs
70o bank = approximately 3 Gs
Stall Speed
Stall speed increases in proportion to the square root of the load factor
Ex. In a 3G turn, a plane that normally stalls at 50 KIAS will stall at about 85 knots

The airplane will stall at a higher indicated airspeed when excessive maneuvering loads are imposed
Smoothly and positively apply the control pressures to execute the chandelle
Abrupt, aggressive control inputs could lead to an accelerated stall

As the turn radius gets smaller, a difference develops between the speed of the inside & outside wing
Outside wing travels a longer path in the same amount of time as the inside wing, and thus generates more lift
Difference in lift can increase bank
Shallow Bank: Lift differential is overcome by lateral stability
Medium Bank: Lift differential matches lateral stability
High Bank: Lift differential outweighs lateral stability
Aircraft continues to bank even with neutral flight controls
Aileron pressure is required in the direction opposite the turn to maintain bank angle
Overbanking Tendency & the Chandelle
Opposite aileron is necessary in the slow, nose high turn near the top of the Chandelle to prevent overbanking
RM: Turn Rate & Radius 									AI.IX.C.R7
Turn Rate: Degrees per second the aircraft is turning
Affected by both the bank angle and airspeed
As bank angle increases, so does the rate of turn
As airspeed increases, the rate of turn decreases
Turn Radius: Size of circle an aircraft would fly during a turn
Also affected by both the bank angle and airspeed – but opposite to turn rate
As bank angle increases, the radius of turn decreases
As airspeed increases, the radius of turn increases
Confined Area Operations
Minimizing radius and maximizing turn rate provides the most confined area for a turn
Higher bank and slower airspeed
Maximum Performance

The plane should gain the most altitude possible for a degree of bank and power setting without stalling – However, since numerous variables affect the amount of altitude gained, altitude gained is not a criterion on the quality of the chandelle
RM: Energy Management 									AI.IX.C.R6
If pitch is increased too little or too slowly, climb performance is limited
If pitch is increased too high, or too quickly, the aircraft will stall before completion
Energy must be balanced to maximize performance

Before Starting
Select an altitude – no lower than 1,500’ AGL
Pre-maneuver checklist; clear the area
Straight-and-level at VA, with flaps/gear UP
Note/bug the heading
Rollout will be on the reciprocal heading
Choose a visual reference point 90o off the wing in the direction of the turn
First 90o – Constant Bank, Changing Pitch
Smoothly Enter a Coordinated 30o Turn
Maintain 30o of bank until 90o point
Adjust for variations/overbanking tendency
As speed decreases, overbanking increases
Apply Max Power & Initiate a Climbing Turn
Maintain bank angle and coordination as power is increased
No other power adjustments are made during the maneuver
Smoothly apply back pressure to reach the highest pitch attitude as 90o of the turn is completed
Intent is to be halfway between entry speed and min controllable airspeed at 90o point
Divide attention between visual references, the 90o reference point, and instruments
If the pitch is increased too quickly the aircraft will stall before reaching 180o
If the pitch is increased too slowly, the aircraft will not come close to the stall speed

Right rudder should be gradually increased to control yaw and keep coordinated

90o Point
Airspeed should be about midway between entry speed & minimum controllable speed
Bank is at 30o, pitch is at the highest pitch attitude

Roll out of the Bank at a Constant Rate
Roll out approximately 10o of bank for every 30o of heading change
Keep Pitch Attitude Constant
As airspeed decreases, increased back pressure is required to maintain pitch
Left turning tendencies become more prevalent; right rudder is necessary to remain coordinated
180o Point
Airspeed should just be reaching minimum controllable airspeed
Bank has been reduced to wings level
Pitch is at the highest pitch attitude

Time the rollout so that wings are level at the 180o point
Pitch attitude should be held momentarily while at the minimum controllable airspeed

Common Errors 										AI.IX.C.K5
Not clearing the area
Initial bank is too shallow resulting in a stall
Initial bank is too steep resulting in failure to gain maximum performance
Allowing the bank angle to increase after initial establishment
Not starting the recovery at the 90° point in the turn
Allowing the pitch attitude to increase as the bank is rolled out during the second 90° of turn
Leveling the wings prior to the 180° point being reached
Pitch attitude is low on recovery resulting in airspeed well above stall speed
Application of flight control pressures is not smooth
Poor flight control coordination
Stalling at any point during the maneuver
Execution of a steep turn instead of a climbing maneuver
Not scanning for other traffic during the maneuver
Performing by reference to the instruments rather than visual references
RM: Hazards
RM: Dividing Attention									 AI.IX.C.R1
Crosscheck focus is primarily on outside references with glances inside for airspeed, altitude, etc.
Over concentration inside or outside will result in the other being neglected and a poor maneuver
Allows the pilot to divide attention between aircraft control and orientation
Orientation is not just aircraft attitude, but also where you are and what or who is around you
In the case of an unsafe situation/orientation stop the maneuver and fix the problem – Safety first!
Distractions, SA & Disorientation, Task Prioritization 					AI.IX.C.R4
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop
Focus on aircraft performance and clear for traffic - If distracted, recognize it and fix it – Safety first
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions
Maintain SA
Starts with preflight planning
Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
Divide attention between inside and outside references
If SA is lost, admit it and fix the problem
If disoriented, stop what you’re doing and get to a safe attitude, airspeed, and altitude
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition
Task Management
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
Proper task management can help prevent distractions, loss of SA, and disorientation
Safety is the number one priority – Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Low Altitude Maneuvering 									AI.IX.C.R3
A small problem at high altitude can quickly become a big problem at a low altitude
Be aware of, and avoid, obstructions, towers, etc.
Quick, panicked maneuvers, especially if slow, can result in a stall/loss of control near the ground

A low altitude stall or spin can leave little to no recovery time
ALWAYS maintain coordination, and airspeed at low altitudes
If you get any indication of a stall at low level, recover, and climb to a safe altitude
Spin - A result of a stall + yaw
Prevention
Maintain coordination
Do not use abrupt, excessive pressure inputs (especially back elevator pressure)
Stop whatever you’re doing and recover at the first sign of a stall

Ailerons - Neutral
Rudder - Full rudder opposite the spin direction
Elevator - Brisk, positive forward pressure (nose down)
When the spin stops, neutralize the rudder & raise the nose, being careful not to stall again
Different aircraft respond differently to spins and spin recoveries, follow the POH procedures
CFIT (Controlled Flight into Terrain) - AC 61-134: General Aviation CFIT Awareness
The solution to combating CFIT accidents starts on the ground
Common themes include proper planning, good decision making, and being able to safely operate the aircraft throughout its entire operating range
Recommendations:
Non-instrument rated VFR pilots should not attempt to fly in IMC
Know and fly above minimum published safe altitudes
If IFR, fly published procedures
Verify proper altitude, especially at night or overwater, through use of a correctly set altimeter
Verify all ATC clearances. Question potentially hazardous clearances
Maintain situational awareness both vertically and horizontally
Comply with appropriate regulations for your specific operation
Don't operate below minimum safe altitudes if uncertain of position or ATC clearance
Be extra careful when operating in an area which you are not familiar
Use current charts, appropriate checklists, and know your aircraft and its equipment
Collision Hazards 										AI.IX.C.R2
Collision Avoidance
Scanning
Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Each movement should not exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
Clearing Procedures
Climb/Descent: Use gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Prior to any turn: Clear in the direction of the turn
Maneuvers: Clearing turns – Clear above/below/in front/behind and during maneuvers
Operation Lights On - Voluntary FAA safety program
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night
Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113)
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging Aircraft
Same Category Aircraft: The aircraft to the right has the right-of-way
Different Categories: Basically, the less maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way
Balloons, gliders, and airships have the right of way over airplanes
An aircraft towing or refueling an aircraft has the right-of-way over engine driven aircraft
Approaching Head-on: Each pilot shall alter course to the right
Overtaking: Aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way; when overtaking, pass on the right
Landing
Aircraft landing/on final to land have the right-of-way over those in flight or on the surface
When 2 or more aircraft are approaching for landing, the lower aircraft has the right-of-way
Don’t take advantage of either of these rules

Study terminal charts and IFR/VFR chart altitudes, use Max Elevation Figures (MEFs)
Day vs Night flying over terrain
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late

Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure

Research obstacles near airports (Terminal Procedures, NOTAMs, etc.)
Antenna Towers can reach > 1,000-2,000’ AGL with supporting guys wires 1,500’ horizontally
Overhead Wires (may not be lit) and often span departures & landmarks pilots often follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc.
Conclusion: Brief review of the main point

paragraphs.text: IX.D. Lazy Eights
Introduction
How
Relating the Maneuver
The maneuver can be compared to a half pipe and a transfer of energy
A transfer of energy as we climb the half pipe and then descend on the other side
The energy is used to get to the top, then we ride the ‘pipe’ back down
Crop-dusting maneuver
Performing the Lazy Eight 						AI.IX.D.K1, AI.IX.D.K3, AI.IX.D.K4
Before Starting
Select an altitude – No lower than 1,500’ AGL
Pre-maneuver checklist; Clear the area
Straight-and-level flight, at or below VA (reference any other applicable performance/airspeed limitations)
Choose visual reference points at 45o, 90o, & 135o in the direction of turn
Should be easily identifiable and toward/on the horizon
Starting the Lazy Eight
Begin a gradual climbing turn toward the 45o reference point
Intent is to reach maximum pitch/15o bank at the 45o point
Pitch must be increased faster than bank
As pitch is increased, speed decreases and the rate of turn increases
Since bank is also being increased, the rate of turn is further increasing
Decreasing airspeed means increased torque requiring right rudder
45o Point: Pitch is at the maximum and bank is at 15o
45o to 90o
Bank should continue to increase at the same rate to reach 30o at the 90o point
Opposite aileron may be required to maintain the bank angle (maintain coordination)
Pitch will decrease from maximum to pass through level flight at the 90o point
Decrease at the same rate as the increase in the initial climbing turn
As the aircraft continues to slow, additional right rudder pressure is necessary
Right rudder pressure will be highest at the slowest point (90o point of the turn)
90o Point
Bank should be at the maximum angle (approximately 30o)
Airspeed should be at its minimum (5 to 10 knots above the stall speed)
Pitch should be passing through level flight
90o to 135o
Airplane should be flown into a descending turn
Nose should describe the same size loop below the horizon as it did above
Bank is consistently decreased to reach 15o of bank at the 135o turn point
Pitch is decreased to reach the maximum pitch down at 135o of turn
Guide the nose down, don’t dive
Max pitch down is less than max pitch
Gravity, thrust, and forward component of lift work together to descend the aircraft
As airspeed increases, right rudder pressure will need to be relaxed
135o Point: Pitch is at the minimum and bank is at 15o
135o to 180o
Continue to decrease bank to level the wings at the 180o point
Increase pitch to bring the nose back to the horizon
Bank and pitch should reach straight-and-level flight at the 180o point
Note the amount of turn remaining and adjust the rate of rollout / pitch
As airspeed continues to increase, reduce rudder and aileron pressure
Altitude should be where the maneuver was started
180o point
Upon returning to the starting altitude and the 180o point, a climbing turn should be started immediately in the opposite direction using the same visual references
The second turn should mimic the first as closely as possible
RM: Dividing Attention 									AI.IX.D.R1
Crosscheck focus is primarily on outside references with glances inside for airspeed, altitude, etc.
Over concentration inside or outside will result in the other being neglected and a poor maneuver
Allows the pilot to divide attention between aircraft control and orientation
Orientation is not just bank/pitch attitude, but also where you are & what or who is around you
In the case of an unsafe situation or orientation stop the maneuver and fix the problem. Safety first
RM: Energy Management 									AI.IX.D.R6
Unsymmetrical Eights
A lazy eight should consist of two symmetrical 180-degree turns, in opposite directions
A failure to manage energy leads to unsymmetrical turns. Differences between the turns can include:
Differing pitch attitudes and/or bank angles
Differing rate of pitch and/or bank
Uncoordinated flight
Altitude Changes
If excess power is used, the aircraft will have gained altitude at the end of the maneuver
If insufficient power is used, the aircraft will have lost altitude
Reference Appendix A. Energy Management as needed for more detailed energy management concepts – Corresponding slides can be found in the slide’s appendix
Overbanking Tendency 									AI.IX.D.K2
As the turn radius gets smaller, a difference develops between the speed of the inside & outside wing
Outside wing travels a longer path in the same amount of time as the inside wing, and thus generates more lift
Difference in lift can increase bank
Shallow Bank: Lift differential is overcome by lateral stability
Medium Bank: Lift differential matches lateral stability
High Bank: Lift differential outweighs lateral stability
Aircraft continues to bank even with neutral flight controls
Aileron pressure is required in the direction opposite the turn to maintain bank angle
Overbanking Tendency & the Lazy Eight
In a nose high turn at a slow airspeed, as at the top of the lazy eight, bank will continue to increase
Use opposite aileron to maintain desired bank angle and prevent overbanking
Most noticeable at 90o
RM: Rudder Control (RM: Uncoordinated flight) 				AI.IX.D.K2, AI.IX.D.R5
As airspeed decreases, right rudder is gradually applied to counter left turning tendencies
Pressure is the greatest at the point of lowest airspeed
More right rudder is needed in the right turn – compensates for adverse yaw + left turn tendencies
In the left turn, the adverse yaw counteracts some of the left turning tendencies
Climbing Right Turn: Controls are slightly crossed due to overbanking tendency/left turning tendencies
Remain coordinated, this is fine
Summary
The maneuver requires constantly changing control pressures
It is not possible to perform it mechanically
Divide attention between visual references, reference points, pitch, bank, airspeed, & coordination
Talk through the maneuver – know what you’re going to do at each 45o point
Use smooth, controlled inputs to obtain constant rate pitch and bank changes - Don’t be aggressive
Common Errors 										AI.IX.D.K5
Not clearing the area
Maneuver is not symmetrical across each 180°
Inadequate or improper selection or use of 45°, 90°, 135° references
Ineffective planning
Gain or loss of altitude at each 180° point
Poor control at the top of each climb segment resulting in the pitch rapidly falling through the horizon
Airspeed or bank angle standards not met
Control roughness
Poor flight control coordination
Stalling at any point during the maneuver
Execution of a steep turn instead of a climbing maneuver
Not scanning for other traffic during the maneuver
Performing by reference to the flight instruments rather than visual references
RM: Hazards
Accelerated Stalls 										AI.IX.D.R7
The aircraft stalls at a higher indicated airspeed when excessive maneuvering loads are imposed on it
Pitching and rolling actions tend to be more sudden
Recovery
Promptly release back pressure, increase power, return to straight and level coordinated flight
Accelerated Stalls and Lazy Eights
Use smooth, controlled inputs. Avoid aggressive/large control inputs especially close to the ground
Fly it as described, Lazy
Dividing Attention 										AI.IX.D.R1
Crosscheck focuses primarily on outside references with glances inside for airspeed, altitude, etc.
Constantly changing control forces requires effective attention management
Divide attention between aircraft control and orientation
Orientation is not just aircraft attitude, but also where you are and what or who is around you
In the case of an unsafe situation or orientation stop the maneuver and fix the problem. Safety first!
Distractions, SA & Disorientation, Task Prioritization 					AI.IX.D.R4
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop
Focus on aircraft performance and clear for traffic - If distracted, recognize it and fix it – Safety first
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions
Maintain SA
Starts with preflight planning
Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
Divide attention between inside and outside references
If SA is lost, admit it and fix the problem
If disoriented, stop what you’re doing and get to a safe attitude, airspeed, and altitude
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition
Task Management
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
Proper task management can help prevent distractions, loss of SA, and disorientation
Safety is the number one priority – Aviate, Navigate, Communicate

A small problem at high altitude can quickly become a big problem at a low altitude
Be aware of, and avoid, obstructions, towers, etc.
Quick, panicked maneuvers, especially if slow, can result in a stall/loss of control near the ground
Low Altitude Stall/Spin
A low altitude stall or spin can leave little to no recovery time
ALWAYS maintain coordination, and airspeed at low altitudes
If you get any indication of a stall at low level, recover, and climb to a safe altitude
Spin - A result of a stall + yaw
Prevention
Maintain coordination
Do not use abrupt, excessive pressure inputs (especially back elevator pressure)
Stop whatever you’re doing and recover at the first sign of a stall
Recovery (PARE)
Power - Idle
Ailerons - Neutral
Rudder - Full rudder opposite the spin direction
Elevator - Brisk, positive forward pressure (nose down)
When the spin stops, neutralize the rudder & raise the nose, being careful not to stall again
Different aircraft respond differently to spins and spin recoveries, follow the POH procedures

The solution to combating CFIT accidents starts on the ground
Common themes include proper planning, good decision making, and being able to safely operate the aircraft throughout its entire operating range

Non-instrument rated VFR pilots should not attempt to fly in IMC

If IFR, fly published procedures

Verify all ATC clearances. Question potentially hazardous clearances

Comply with appropriate regulations for your specific operation

Be extra careful when operating in an area which you are not familiar
Use current charts, appropriate checklists, and know your aircraft and its equipment

Collision Avoidance

Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field

An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging Aircraft

Don’t take advantage of either of these rules

Day vs Night flying over terrain
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late

Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
Obstacles & Wire Strike

Antenna Towers can reach > 1,000-2,000’ AGL with supporting guys wires 1,500’ horizontally
Overhead Wires (may not be lit) and often span departures & landmarks pilots often follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc.
Conclusion: Brief review of the main point

WHAT
A maneuver consisting of two 180o turns in opposite directions, while making a climb and descent in a symmetrical pattern during each of the turns. 
It is the only standard flight training maneuver during which at no time do the forces on the controls remain constant.

The lazy eight develops proper coordination of the controls through a wide range of airspeeds and attitudes. It is a great trainer because of the constantly varying forces and attitudes required.  It also helps develop subconscious feel, planning, orientation, coordination, and sense of speed.

Antenna Towers can reach > 1,000-2,000’ AGL with supporting guys wires 1,500’ horizontally

How
Purpose

It is more sensible to practice at the traffic pattern limit of 30o of bank to establish good habits

Turn Rate
Degrees per second the aircraft is turning
Affected by both the bank angle and airspeed
As bank angle increases, so does the rate of turn
As airspeed increases, the rate of turn decreases
Turn Radius
Size of circle an aircraft would fly during a turn
Also affected by both the bank angle and airspeed (but opposite to Rate of Turn)
As bank angle increases, the radius of turn decreases
As airspeed increases, the radius of turn increases

Crab: With any crosswind, the airplane will have to be crabbed into the wind
Use coordinated flight controls to point the aircraft into the wind; adjust crab for wind strength
Roll Rate: Adjust roll rate to prevent drifting closer or farther from the desired course
If wind pushes the plane toward the course, the roll rate should be slow
If wind pushes the airplane away from the course, the roll rate should he high
Bank Angle: Amount of bank varies with groundspeed
Higher Groundspeeds (tailwind): Requires steeper bank to maintain the track
Slower Groundspeeds (headwind): Require a shallower bank to maintain the track
As groundspeed changes during a turn, bank will have to change with it
If groundspeed decreases through the turn, bank should decrease through the turn
If groundspeed increases through the turn, bank should increase through the turn

The airplane must always remain in coordinated flight

Keep airspeed in your crosscheck. Increase or decrease power as necessary

Allows the pilot to divide attention between aircraft control and orientation
Orientation is not just the bank/pitch attitude, but also where you are & what/who is around you

Bank: Groundspeed increases through the turn so bank increases through the turn
Strongest headwind / slowest groundspeed at the start requires the shallowest bank
Bank increases to medium as headwind changes to crosswind / groundspeed increases

Roll Out/Amount of Turn

In a perfect scenario, drift is not encountered on the upwind/downwind legs
Difficult to find a situation where the wind is blowing exactly parallel to the boundaries
Common Errors 										AI.IX.E.K5
Failure to adequately clear the surrounding area for safety hazards, initially & throughout the maneuver
Failure to establish a constant, level altitude prior to entering the maneuver.
Failure to maintain altitude during the maneuver.
Failure to properly assess wind direction.
Failure to establish the appropriate wind correction angle.
Failure to apply coordinated aileron and rudder pressure, resulting in slips and skids.
Failure to manipulate the flight controls in a smooth and continuous manner.
Failure to properly divide attention between airplane control and orientation with ground references.
Failure to execute turns with accurate timing.
RM: Hazards
Distractions, SA & Disorientation, Task Prioritization 					AI.IX.E.R4
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop
Focus on aircraft performance and clear for traffic - If distracted, recognize it and fix it – Safety first
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions
Maintain SA
Starts with preflight planning
Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
Divide attention between inside and outside references
If SA is lost, admit it and fix the problem
If disoriented, stop what you’re doing and get to a safe attitude, airspeed, and altitude
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition
Task Management
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
Proper task management can help prevent distractions, loss of SA, and disorientation
Safety is the number one priority – Aviate, Navigate, Communicate

A small problem at high altitude can quickly become a big problem at a low altitude
Be aware of, and avoid, obstructions, towers, etc.
Quick, panicked maneuvers, especially if slow, can result in a stall/loss of control near the ground

If you get any indication of a stall at low level, recover, and climb to a safe altitude

Maintain coordination
Do not use abrupt, excessive pressure inputs (especially back elevator pressure)
Stop whatever you’re doing and recover at the first sign of a stall

Ailerons - Neutral
Rudder - Full rudder opposite the spin direction
Elevator - Brisk, positive forward pressure (nose down)

Different aircraft respond differently to spins and spin recoveries, follow the POH procedures
CFIT (Controlled Flight into Terrain) - AC 61-134: General Aviation CFIT Awareness
The solution to combating CFIT accidents starts on the ground
Common themes include proper planning, good decision making, and being able to safely operate the aircraft throughout its entire operating range
Recommendations:
Non-instrument rated VFR pilots should not attempt to fly in IMC
Know and fly above minimum published safe altitudes
If IFR, fly published procedures
Verify proper altitude, especially at night or overwater, through use of a correctly set altimeter
Verify all ATC clearances. Question potentially hazardous clearances
Maintain situational awareness both vertically and horizontally
Comply with appropriate regulations for your specific operation
Don't operate below minimum safe altitudes if uncertain of position or ATC clearance
Be extra careful when operating in an area which you are not familiar
Use current charts, appropriate checklists, and know your aircraft and its equipment
Collision Hazards 										AI.IX.E.R2
Collision Avoidance
Scanning
Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Each movement should not exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
Clearing Procedures
Climb/Descent: Use gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Prior to any turn: Clear in the direction of the turn
Maneuvers: Clearing turns – Clear above/below/in front/behind and during maneuvers
Operation Lights On - Voluntary FAA safety program
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night
Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113)
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging Aircraft
Same Category Aircraft: The aircraft to the right has the right-of-way
Different Categories: Basically, the less maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way
Balloons, gliders, and airships have the right of way over airplanes
An aircraft towing or refueling an aircraft has the right-of-way over engine driven aircraft
Approaching Head-on: Each pilot shall alter course to the right
Overtaking: Aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way; when overtaking, pass on the right

Aircraft landing/on final to land have the right-of-way over those in flight or on the surface
When 2 or more aircraft are approaching for landing, the lower aircraft has the right-of-way
Don’t take advantage of either of these rules
Terrain
Study terminal charts and IFR/VFR chart altitudes, use Max Elevation Figures (MEFs)
Day vs Night flying over terrain
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
Obstacles & Wire Strike
Research obstacles near airports (Terminal Procedures, NOTAMs, etc.)
Antenna Towers can reach > 1,000-2,000’ AGL with supporting guys wires 1,500’ horizontally
Overhead Wires (may not be lit) and often span departures & landmarks pilots often follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc.
Conclusion: Brief review of the main point

Rate of Turn (degrees per second the aircraft is turning)
Affected by both the bank angle and airspeed
As bank angle increases, so does the rate of turn
As airspeed increases, the rate of turn decreases
Radius of Turn (size of circle an aircraft would fly during a turn)
Also affected by both the bank angle and airspeed (but opposite to Rate of Turn)
As bank angle increases, the radius of turn decreases
As airspeed increases, the radius of turn increases
Maintaining a Constant Radius: Bank, roll, and crab are adjusted for wind and changing groundspeed
Roll Rate: Adjusted to prevent drifting in or out of the constant radius course

Low Roll Rate: When wind will push you toward the reference / at a low groundspeed

The aircraft will have to be crabbed into any crosswind to maintain a constant radius
Increases from start of the turn to 90o point (strongest crosswind), then decreases to the rollout
First turn: crab into the turn; Second turn: crab out of the turn
The stronger the crosswind, the greater the wind correction angle

Prior to Entry
Selecting a Suitable Altitude
Entry altitude should be 600’ - 1,000’ AGL per the ACS
± 100’ restrictions (800’ AGL is a good balance with room above/below the requirement)
Selecting a Suitable Reference Line
Estimate wind direction (METAR, smoke, water, trees, fields, or a 360o turn noting ground track)
Select a straight-line ground reference perpendicular to the wind (Roads, train tracks, fences, etc.)

High Groundspeed: Roll into the turn must be rapid, and the angle of bank the steepest

As the turn progresses and airspeed decreases, bank angle must be decreased
Otherwise, the turn would get progressively tighter as groundspeed decreased
Wind correction angle increases through the first 90o of turn, decreases through the second
Max crosswind correction angle should occur at the 90o crosswind point
Correction angle varies with wind strength - crab into the turn

Reference the nose / wingtips, and ground reference to adjust the rollout to cross the reference line wings level, opposite the entry heading, on altitude and airspeed
Upwind Side of the Turn (2nd Half) - Crossing the reference, start a turn in the opposite direction

Low Groundspeed: Roll into the turn must be slow, and the angle of bank the shallowest
Normal rate will keep you too close to the reference line; won’t complete 180o turn
As the turn progresses and airspeed increases, bank angle must increase
Wind correction increases through the first 90o of turn, and decreases through the second
Max crosswind correction angle should occur at the 90o crosswind point
Correction angle varies with wind strength – crab out of the turn

Time the rollout to reach straight-and-level flight over / perpendicular to the reference line
Judge the closure rate and increase bank to cross wings level
Maintaining a Constant Altitude (± 100’ per the ACS)
Trim for level flight prior to starting the maneuver
As bank increases, back elevator pressure will need to be increased to maintain altitude
Divide attention, don’t fixate on any one thing

A constant power setting and a stable altitude go a long way in maintaining a constant airspeed
Power may have to be added with increased bank / back pressure and vice versa

Quick, panicked maneuvers, especially if slow, can result in a stall/loss of control near the ground

Collision Avoidance
Scanning

An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging Aircraft
Same Category Aircraft: The aircraft to the right has the right-of-way
Different Categories: Basically, the less maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way
Balloons, gliders, and airships have the right of way over airplanes

Turn Rate
Degrees per second the aircraft is turning
Affected by both the bank angle and airspeed
As bank angle increases, so does the rate of turn
As airspeed increases, the rate of turn decreases
Turn Radius
Size of circle an aircraft would fly during a turn
Also affected by both the bank angle and airspeed (but opposite to Rate of Turn)
As bank angle increases, the radius of turn decreases
As airspeed increases, the radius of turn increases
Wind Correction
Roll Rate
Adjusted to prevent drifting in/out of the desired radius
High Roll Rate: When wind will push you away from the reference / at a high groundspeed
Low Roll Rate: When wind will push you toward the reference / at a low groundspeed
Bank Angle
High groundspeeds (tailwind) require high bank
Low groundspeeds (headwind) require low bank
Wind Correction Angle (WCA)
The aircraft will have to be crabbed into any crosswind to maintain a constant radius
The stronger the crosswind, the greater the wind correction angle
WCA increases from start to 90o point, then decreases to 180o point, and repeats on the other side
First Half of the 360: Crab into the turn
Second Half: Crab out of the turn
Coordination
Maintain coordination – Do not use rudder to “help” the turn, or force a crab

If there were no wind, bank would be constant around the turn, with no need to crab

Divide attention between the reference point, aircraft, what’s coming next, and the surroundings

Prior to Entry
Select an Altitude

Select a Reference Point
Prominent and easily distinguishable but also small enough for precise reference (Ex. crossroads)

Helps to orient with the wind & ensure the airplane is in the right place at the right time
Clear of populated areas, obstructions, hazards
Allows for an emergency landing, if necessary
Pre-Maneuver Checklist; Clear the area
Airspeed: At or below VA - Trimmed for hands off level flight
Entry Procedure
Enter on the downwind approximately ¼ to ½ mile abeam the point (note entry heading for orientation)

Coordinated roll in to maintain the desired radius
Steepest bank angle and high roll rate – bank should not exceed 45o
As bank increases, increase back pressure to maintain altitude
First Half of the Turn (Downwind Half)
Decreasing Groundspeed: Begins with a tailwind transitioning to a crosswind then a headwind
Steepest Bank Transitioning to the Shallowest Bank
As airspeed decreases, bank should be gradually reduced to maintain a constant radius
As bank is reduced, back pressure should be relaxed to maintain altitude
Crab Inside the Turn
Progressively crab inside the turn to establish max wind correction angle at the 90o point
Decrease wind correction angle from the 90o point until completing the first half of the turn

As bank is reduced, rudder pressure is also reduced
Completing the 1st Half of the Turn
Bank should be at its lowest and crab should be removed
Direct headwind, therefore lowest groundspeed, and lowest bank angle/no crab required
Second Half of the Turn (Upwind Half) – Opposite of the 1st half
Increasing Groundspeed: Begins with a headwind transitioning to a crosswind then a tailwind
Shallowest Bank Transitioning back to the Steepest Bank
As airspeed increases, bank should gradually increase to maintain a constant radius
As bank is increased, back pressure should increase to maintain altitude
Crab Outside the Turn
Progressively crab outside the turn to establish max wind correction angle at the 90o point
Decrease wind correction angle from the 90o point until completing the first half of the turn
RM: Coordination									AI.IX.E.R5
As bank is increased, rudder pressure is also increased
Completing the 2nd Half of the Turn
Bank should be the highest (same as entry bank angle)

Failure to properly execute constant radius turns.

paragraphs.text: IX.F. Eights on Pylons
Introduction
How
What is Pivotal Altitude (PA)									AI.IX.F.K3
Altitude which keeps a pylon in the same position relative to the aircraft as the plane turns around it
Varies with groundspeed
The reference line is parallel with the lateral axis (off wingtip or position on the window)
When turning at PA, the reference line appears to be fixed to a point on the landscape
Above the pivotal altitude, the wingtip appears to move backward
Below the pivotal altitude, the wingtip appears to move forward
The Basics 										AI.IX.F.K2, AI.IX.F.K3
Pivotal Altitude is Based on Groundspeed
As groundspeed increases, pivotal altitude increases, and vice versa
Does not change with bank angle
Distance from pylon affects bank angle
Circling the reference point, groundspeed, & therefore pivotal altitude, will change with wind
To adjust, the pilot climbs or descends to maintain the visual reference with the pylon
The change in altitude will depend on how much the wind affects groundspeed
Maintaining the Pivotal Altitude References
Pitch
As Groundspeed Decreases, Pivotal Altitude Decreases
The wing moves backward over the ground & the point moves forward in relation to the wing
Descend to maintain the reference line to the pylon
We descend to lower pivotal altitude, increase in airspeed moves pivotal altitude up
Rule: If the point moves FORWARD, apply FORWARD pressure
As Groundspeed Increases, Pivotal Altitude Increases
Wing moves forward over the ground / point moves backward in relation to the wing
Climb to maintain the reference line to the pylon
We climb to higher pivotal altitude, decrease in airspeed moves pivotal altitude down
Rule: If the point moves BACKWARD, apply BACK pressure
Corrections & Wind Speed
Corrections are like tracking a VOR
Once the correction is made (intercept angle is established), remove the correction when the pylon is back on the line-of-sight reference (intercepting the radial)
Changes in pitch & altitude are based on wind speed
The stronger the wind, the greater the variation in max/min pivotal altitudes
Too strong of winds becomes unsafe
PA gets closer and closer to the ground and can require very high bank angles
RM: Coordination	 								AI.IX.F.R5
Always maintain coordinated flight
Use altitude changes, not rudder pressure, to hold the reference point on the pylon
Bank
Performed at bank angles ranging from shallow to steep (no more than 40o per the ACS)
Distance from the pylon affects bank
As wind pushes you to or from the pylons, bank is used to maintain the reference line
If the pylon moves above the reference point, (i.e., above the wing tip) decrease bank
If the pylon moves below the reference point (i.e., below the wing tip), increase bank
RM: Energy Management & Power         							AI.IX.F.R6
Pivotal altitude is based on groundspeed
Set power prior to entering the maneuver to keep the desired indicated airspeed consistent
Changes in power lead to changes in airspeed which change pivotal altitude
The more consistent the power setting, the more consistent the airspeed
Reference Appendix A. Energy Management as needed for more detailed energy management concepts – Corresponding slides can be found in the slide’s appendix
Calculating Pivotal Altitude 			          					AI.IX.F.K3
Equation to estimate pivotal altitude
For Knots – ) + MSL
For MPH – () + MSL
Calculate the highest and lowest pivotal altitudes
Highest = TAS + tailwind; Lowest = TAS - headwind
If altitudes are unsafe, do not perform the maneuver
Performing Eights on Pylons 							AI.IX.F.K1, AI.IX.F.K5
Selecting the Pylons
Two ground points along a line perpendicular to the wind
Sufficiently prominent & easy to see in an open area away from hills/obstructions
Smaller pylons are easier to notice changes in movement
About ½ mile apart (3-5 second flight between pylons)
Allows time for planning, but not unnecessary drone between the pylons
At the same elevation
RM: Ensure a suitable emergency landing area within gliding distance			AI.IX.F.R7
Pre-Maneuver
Pre-maneuver checklist; Clear the area of traffic
Trimmed for straight and level flight, at or below VA
Entry
Fly to the midpoint of the pylons at a 45o angle to the downwind (note the entry heading)
Technique: Make the first turn to the left around the left pylon (out your window)
Downwind entry starts at the highest groundspeed & therefore the highest pivotal altitude
Lower the upwind wing to roll into a 30-40o bank when the pylon is just ahead of the reference
Place wingtip (or other reference) at the base of the pylon
First Turn
Entry is at the Highest Groundspeed & Highest Pivotal Altitude
As the groundspeed decreases through the turn, pivotal altitude decreases
With no corrections, the pylon will move forward
Forward movement = forward pressure – Descend to maintain reference point
Decrease bank to maintain reference as wind pushes the airplane away from the point
Continuing the Turn
Continuing around, groundspeed and therefore pivotal altitude will begin to increase again
Climb to maintain pivotal altitude & the visual reference – Backward movement = back pressure
Relative wind will push the airplane toward the pylon 					AI.IX.F.K4
Increase bank angle to maintain the visual reference
Transitioning between Pylons
Start the rollout to proceed diagonally to a point on the downwind side of the 2nd pylon
Maintain straight and level flight for 3 to 5 seconds
Crab into the wind to correct for wind drift 						AI.IX.F.K4
Initiate a turn in the opposite direction as the pylon aligns with the reference point
Roll into 30-40o bank and place the same reference on the other side of the plane on the pylon
Second Turn
Same procedures as the first turn, but in the opposite direction
Entry is at the highest ground speed – As groundspeed decreases, descend to maintain PA
Continuing through the turn, groundspeed increases again – climb to maintain PA
Exit
Roll wings level after completing one rotation around each pylon and exit on the entry heading
Common Errors										 AI.IX.F.K6
Failure to adequately clear the surrounding area for safety hazards, initially and throughout the maneuver
Skidding or slipping in turns (whether trying to hold the pylon with rudder or not)
Excessive gain or loss of altitude
Poor choice of pylons
Not entering the pylon turns into the wind
Failure to compensate for drift when flying between pylons
Failure to time the bank so that the turn entry is completed with the pylon in position
Abrupt control usage
Inability to select pivotal altitude
RM: Hazards
Division of Attention 										AI.IX.F.R1
Crosscheck focuses primarily on outside references with glances inside for airspeed, altitude, etc.
Over concentration inside or outside will result in the other being neglected and a poor maneuver
Allows the pilot to divide attention between aircraft control and orientation
Orientation is not just airplane attitude, but also where you are & what/who is around you
In the case of an unsafe situation or orientation stop the maneuver and fix the problem. Safety first
Don’t fixate, divide attention between the turn, wind, flying the aircraft, and your surroundings
Be proactive in making corrections
Distractions, SA & Disorientation, Task Prioritization 					AI.IX.F.R4
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop
Focus on aircraft performance and clear for traffic - If distracted, recognize it and fix it – Safety first
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions
Maintain SA
Starts with preflight planning
Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
Divide attention between inside and outside references
If SA is lost, admit it and fix the problem
If disoriented, stop what you’re doing and get to a safe attitude, airspeed, and altitude
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition
Task Management
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
Proper task management can help prevent distractions, loss of SA, and disorientation
Safety is the number one priority – Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Low Altitude Maneuvering 									AI.IX.F.R3
A small problem at high altitude can quickly become a big problem at a low altitude
Be aware of, and avoid, obstructions, towers, etc.
Quick, panicked maneuvers, especially if slow, can result in a stall/loss of control near the ground
Low Altitude Stall/Spin
A low altitude stall or spin can leave little to no recovery time
ALWAYS maintain coordination, and airspeed at low altitudes
If you get any indication of a stall at low level, recover, and climb to a safe altitude
Spin - A result of a stall + yaw
Prevention
Maintain coordination
Do not use abrupt, excessive pressure inputs (especially back elevator pressure)
Stop whatever you’re doing and recover at the first sign of a stall
Recovery (PARE)
Power - Idle
Ailerons - Neutral
Rudder - Full rudder opposite the spin direction
Elevator - Brisk, positive forward pressure (nose down)
When the spin stops, neutralize the rudder & raise the nose, being careful not to stall again
Different aircraft respond differently to spins and spin recoveries, follow the POH procedures
CFIT (Controlled Flight into Terrain) - AC 61-134: General Aviation CFIT Awareness
The solution to combating CFIT accidents starts on the ground
Common themes include proper planning, good decision making, and being able to safely operate the aircraft throughout its entire operating range
Recommendations:
Non-instrument rated VFR pilots should not attempt to fly in IMC
Know and fly above minimum published safe altitudes
If IFR, fly published procedures
Verify proper altitude, especially at night or overwater, through use of a correctly set altimeter
Verify all ATC clearances. Question potentially hazardous clearances
Maintain situational awareness both vertically and horizontally
Comply with appropriate regulations for your specific operation
Don't operate below minimum safe altitudes if uncertain of position or ATC clearance
Be extra careful when operating in an area which you are not familiar
Use current charts, appropriate checklists, and know your aircraft and its equipment
Collision Hazards 										AI.IX.F.R2
Collision Avoidance
Scanning
Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Each movement should not exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
Clearing Procedures
Climb/Descent: Use gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Prior to any turn: Clear in the direction of the turn
Maneuvers: Clearing turns – Clear above/below/in front/behind and during maneuvers
Operation Lights On - Voluntary FAA safety program
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night

An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging Aircraft
Same Category Aircraft: The aircraft to the right has the right-of-way
Different Categories: Basically, the less maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way
Balloons, gliders, and airships have the right of way over airplanes
An aircraft towing or refueling an aircraft has the right-of-way over engine driven aircraft
Approaching Head-on: Each pilot shall alter course to the right
Overtaking: Aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way; when overtaking, pass on the right
Landing
Aircraft landing/on final to land have the right-of-way over those in flight or on the surface
When 2 or more aircraft are approaching for landing, the lower aircraft has the right-of-way
Don’t take advantage of either of these rules
Terrain
Study terminal charts and IFR/VFR chart altitudes, use Max Elevation Figures (MEFs)
Day vs Night flying over terrain
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
Obstacles & Wire Strike
Research obstacles near airports (Terminal Procedures, NOTAMs, etc.)
Antenna Towers can reach > 1,000-2,000’ AGL with supporting guys wires 1,500’ horizontally
Overhead Wires (may not be lit) and often span departures & landmarks pilots often follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc.
Conclusion: Brief review of the main point

WHAT
Eights on Pylons involves flying the plane in a figure eight path around two selected points on the ground. The goal is to have an imaginary line extending from the pilot’s eyes to the pylon. The line must be imagined to be parallel to the lateral axis. Along this line, the airplane appears to pivot as it turns around the pylon. No attempt is made to maintain a uniform distance from the pylon.
In other words, if a string extended from the plane to the pylon, the string would remain parallel to the lateral axis as the plane turned around the pylon.

The objective of this maneuver is to develop the ability to maneuver the airplane accurately while dividing one’s attention between the flight path and the selected points on the ground.  Eights on Pylons are extremely helpful in teaching, developing, and testing subconscious control of the airplane.

Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Each movement should not exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
